Round-Up Ready seed allows farmers to utilize far better soil management practices, in addition to far fer chemicals. In the 80's, the standard planting practice would be something like this:

  1. Till up the whole farm (loosening up the top soil, and a major cause of soil run-off), then...
  2. Saturate the field with methyl bromide, which was nasty shit and would kill absolutely everything - weeds, grubs, worms, pests and beneficial insects alike, anything and everything would be wiped out
  3. After the fumigation dissipated, farmers would plow and plant and hope their crops would grow faster than the weeds, but many times they wouldn't. If they had weed issues, they'd need to spray herbicide (carefully spray I might add, as whatever they'd use would kill crops and the weeds alike, and the invaded acres would be a total loss). Depending on the climate, the whether or hundreds of other factors, farmer would have to spray multiple times a season.

Nowadays, most farmers don't till at all. They harvest, let the stalks, roots, etc. die off and act as compost while their fields were fallow in the winter and early Spring. They skip tilling and go strait to plowing and plant as a first step (keeping all the beneficial insects and solidity of the soil 100% intact). They let their fields go for a couple of months, allowing crops and weeds grow to a certain height, then apply one treatment of Round-Up (or any other herbicide they like... it's definitely not the only herbicide available, it's just generally the cheapest, most effective and least toxic option). The Round-Up-Ready crop is immune to the spray, but the weeds all die off. What you're left with is acre after acre of the beneficial crop, no weeds at all, which are of a certain height that they create a sunshade that generally prevents any new weeds from growing back before harvest.

So, given what I've seen from standard farming practice, there's no inherent benefit to using 400% more Round Up and I can't think of a way it would be cost beneficial for any farmer.
